claim: In allergic asthma, allergen inhalation leads to local Th2 cell activation and peribronchial inflammation.
source: In allergic asthma, allergen inhalation leads to local Th2 cell activation and peribronchial inflammation.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about allergic asthma pathophysiology.

claim: Soluble antigens in the bronchial airway lumen were efficiently captured and presented by a population of CD11c+ interstitial macrophages with high CX3CR1-GFP and MHC class II expression.
source: By two-photon microscopy of the mouse lung, we established that soluble antigens in the bronchial airway lumen were efficiently captured and presented by a population of CD11c+ interstitial macrophages with high CX3CR1-GFP and MHC class II expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon microscopy experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: These cells are referred to as Bronchus-Associated Macrophages (BAMs) based on their localization underneath the bronchial epithelium.
source: We refer to these cells as Bronchus-Associated Macrophages (BAMs) based on their localization underneath the bronchial epithelium.
evidence: This is a nomenclature definition based on the observed anatomical localization of the cells.

claim: BAMs were enriched in collagen-rich regions near some airway branchpoints, where inhaled antigens are likely to deposit.
source: BAMs were enriched in collagen-rich regions near some airway branchpoints, where inhaled antigens are likely to deposit.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data showing BAM localization and inference about antigen deposition based on airflow dynamics.

claim: BAMs engaged in extended interactions with effector Th2 cells and promoted Th2 cytokine production.
source: BAMs engaged in extended interactions with effector Th2 cells and promoted Th2 cytokine production.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data and in vitro co-culture experiments showing T cell activation.

claim: BAMs were also often in contact with dendritic cells (DCs).
source: BAMs were also often in contact with dendritic cells (DCs).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations showing physical contacts between BAMs and DCs.

claim: After exposure to inflammatory stimuli, DCs migrated to draining lymph nodes, whereas BAMs remained lung resident.
source: After exposure to inflammatory stimuli, DCs migrated to draining lymph nodes, whereas BAMs remained lung resident.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry, microscopy, and CCR7 expression data showing differential migratory behavior.

claim: BAMs act as local antigen presenting cells in the lung.
source: We propose that BAMs act as local antigen presenting cells in the lung and also transfer antigen to DCs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing antigen capture, processing, presentation, and T cell activation by BAMs.

claim: BAMs transfer antigen to DCs.
source: We propose that BAMs act as local antigen presenting cells in the lung and also transfer antigen to DCs.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on observed contacts between BAMs and DCs and CD169 localization at the interface.

claim: The conducting bronchial airways represent one of the first sites of exposure to inhaled substances and infectious agents.
source: Within the lung, the conducting bronchial airways represent one of the first sites of exposure to inhaled substances and infectious agents.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical and physiological knowledge of the respiratory system.

claim: In allergic asthma, the inhalation of harmless environmental allergens leads to peribronchial inflammation, in which the local activation of type 2 helper T cells (Th2 cells) results in effector cytokine production that promotes pathogenesis.
source: In allergic asthma, the inhalation of harmless environmental allergens leads to peribronchial inflammation, in which the local activation of type 2 helper T cells (Th2 cells) results in effector cytokine production that promotes pathogenesis (Holgate, 2012; Lambrecht et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on asthma pathogenesis.

claim: The Th2 cells are activated by antigen presenting cells (APCs) that survey the epithelial barrier and capture and present antigen.
source: The Th2 cells are activated by antigen presenting cells (APCs) that survey the epithelial barrier and capture and present antigen.
evidence: This is based on established immunological knowledge about T cell activation.

claim: The types of APCs contributing to surveillance of the conducting airways are not fully characterized.
source: However, the types of APCs contributing to surveillance of the conducting airways are not fully characterized, and the anatomical organization that couples antigen capture to Th2 cell activation remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The anatomical organization that couples antigen capture to Th2 cell activation remains unclear.
source: However, the types of APCs contributing to surveillance of the conducting airways are not fully characterized, and the anatomical organization that couples antigen capture to Th2 cell activation remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Unlike alveolar spaces, the conducting airways do not participate in gaseous exchange but serve to conduct and filter air.
source: Unlike alveolar spaces, the conducting airways do not participate in gaseous exchange but serve to conduct and filter air.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical and physiological knowledge of the respiratory system.

claim: As inspired air passes through airway branchpoints, changes in the direction of airflow promote the deposition of particulates and the dissolution of soluble substances in the overlying mucus layer.
source: As inspired air passes through airway branchpoints, changes in the direction of airflow promote the deposition of particulates and the dissolution of soluble substances in the overlying mucus layer (Carvalho et al., 2011; Clarke and Yeates, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on airflow dynamics and particle deposition.

claim: In allergic asthma, eosinophils and lymphocytes are recruited to regions around the conducting airways, resulting in peribronchial inflammation.
source: In allergic asthma, eosinophils and lymphocytes are recruited to regions around the conducting airways, resulting in peribronchial inflammation (Jeffery, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature on asthma pathology.

claim: In several mouse models of airway infections, T and B cells accumulate in organized foci near the airways, forming induced Bronchus-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (BALT) structures.
source: In several mouse models of airway infections, T and B cells accumulate in organized foci near the airways, forming induced Bronchus-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (BALT) structures (Fleige and Förster, 2017; Randall, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on BALT formation.

claim: Most studies have focused on the potential contributions of dendritic cells (DCs) to allergic inflammation in the lung.
source: Most studies have focused on the potential contributions of dendritic cells (DCs) to allergic inflammation in the lung (Wikstrom and Stumbles, 2007), based initially on observations that MHC-II+ cells with dendritic morphology were abundant along both human and rodent airways at baseline (Demedts et al., 2005; Huh et al., 2003; Lambrecht et al., 1998; von Garnier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on DCs in the lung.

claim: MHC-II+ cells with dendritic morphology were abundant along both human and rodent airways at baseline.
source: Most studies have focused on the potential contributions of dendritic cells (DCs) to allergic inflammation in the lung (Wikstrom and Stumbles, 2007), based initially on observations that MHC-II+ cells with dendritic morphology were abundant along both human and rodent airways at baseline (Demedts et al., 2005; Huh et al., 2003; Lambrecht et al., 1998; von Garnier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on airway immune cells.

claim: Flow cytometric analysis of lung-draining lymph nodes, dissociated lung tissue enriched for the conducting airways, and the trachea showed that DCs, gated as CD11c+ MHC-II+ cells, were able to capture, process, and present fluorescent ovalbumin (OVA) administered via the airways.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of lung-draining lymph nodes, dissociated lung tissue enriched for the conducting airways, and the trachea also showed that DCs, gated as CD11c+ MHC-II+ cells, were able to capture, process, and present fluorescent ovalbumin (OVA) administered via the airways (del Rio et al., 2007; Fear et al., 2011; Hammad et al., 2010; Huh et al., 2003; von Garnier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on DC antigen capture.

claim: The uptake of OVA by CD11c+ MHC-II+ cells throughout the lung has been observed by confocal microscopy.
source: The uptake of OVA by CD11c+ MHC-II+ cells throughout the lung has also been observed by confocal microscopy (Hoffmann et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature on antigen uptake.

claim: Two-photon microscopy studies of CD11c-YFP reporter mice found that DCs near the conducting airways did not detectably capture soluble antigens (OVA or dextran), or particulate antigens in the form of beads.
source: however, two-photon microscopy studies of CD11c-YFP reporter mice found that DCs near the conducting airways did not detectably capture soluble antigens (OVA or dextran), or particulate antigens in the form of beads (Thornton et al., 2012; Veres et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on DC antigen capture by microscopy.

claim: CD11c-YFP+ DCs were reported to capture beads at the alveoli in a mouse model of asthma, and then were proposed to migrate to tissue regions proximal to the bronchial airways, where T cells are activated.
source: CD11c-YFP+ DCs were reported to capture beads at the alveoli in a mouse model of asthma, and then were proposed to migrate to tissue regions proximal to the bronchial airways, where T cells are activated (Thornton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature on DC migration.

claim: Individuals allergic to aeroallergens had an increased frequency of Th2 cells that preferentially recognized soluble antigen components of aeroallergens, whereas regulatory T cells preferentially recognized particulate antigen components.
source: The presentation of soluble antigens is pertinent because it was reported that individuals allergic to aeroallergens had an increased frequency of Th2 cells that preferentially recognized soluble antigen components of aeroallergens, whereas regulatory T cells preferentially recognized particulate antigen components (Bacher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature on T cell responses to allergens.

claim: In the intestine, soluble antigen in the lumen is efficiently captured by CX3CR1+ macrophages in the lamina propria.
source: In the intestine, soluble antigen in the lumen is efficiently captured by CX3CR1+ macrophages in the lamina propria (Farache et al., 2013a; Farache et al., 2013b; Mazzini et al., 2014; Schulz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on intestinal macrophages.

claim: Intestinal macrophages were found to be distinct from conventional DCs (cDCs) based on functional and behavioral differences.
source: These intestinal macrophages were found to be distinct from conventional DCs (cDCs) based on functional and behavioral differences and were reported to contribute to local intestinal immunity (Hadis et al., 2011; Mazzini et al., 2014; Schreiber et al., 2013; Schulz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on intestinal macrophages.

claim: Intestinal macrophages were reported to contribute to local intestinal immunity.
source: These intestinal macrophages were found to be distinct from conventional DCs (cDCs) based on functional and behavioral differences and were reported to contribute to local intestinal immunity (Hadis et al., 2011; Mazzini et al., 2014; Schreiber et al., 2013; Schulz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on intestinal macrophages.

claim: Recent gene expression and microscopy studies of the lung have identified CX3CR1+ interstitial macrophages (IMs) that are distinct from alveolar macrophages (AMs).
source: Recent gene expression and microscopy studies of the lung have identified CX3CR1+ interstitial macrophages (IMs) that are distinct from alveolar macrophages (AMs). Notably, subpopulation(s) of these IMs express many of the surface markers previously thought to be exclusive to DCs, such as MHC-II and CD11c (Chakarov et al., 2019; Gautier et al., 2012; Gibbings et al., 2017; Sabatel et al., 2017; Schlitzer et al., 2013; Schyns et al., 2019; Ural et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on lung interstitial macrophages.

claim: Subpopulation(s) of IMs express many of the surface markers previously thought to be exclusive to DCs, such as MHC-II and CD11c.
source: Recent gene expression and microscopy studies of the lung have identified CX3CR1+ interstitial macrophages (IMs) that are distinct from alveolar macrophages (AMs). Notably, subpopulation(s) of these IMs express many of the surface markers previously thought to be exclusive to DCs, such as MHC-II and CD11c (Chakarov et al., 2019; Gautier et al., 2012; Gibbings et al., 2017; Sabatel et al., 2017; Schlitzer et al., 2013; Schyns et al., 2019; Ural et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on lung interstitial macrophages.

claim: In the steady state in naïve mice, lung myeloid APCs are primarily positioned underneath the bronchial airway epithelium.
source: Here, we show that in the steady state in naïve mice, lung myeloid APCs are primarily positioned underneath the bronchial airway epithelium and are strategically enriched near some airway branchpoints where inhaled allergens are likely to deposit.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing the localization of myeloid APCs.

claim: Lung myeloid APCs are strategically enriched near some airway branchpoints where inhaled allergens are likely to deposit.
source: Here, we show that in the steady state in naïve mice, lung myeloid APCs are primarily positioned underneath the bronchial airway epithelium and are strategically enriched near some airway branchpoints where inhaled allergens are likely to deposit.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing the localization of myeloid APCs and inference about allergen deposition.

claim: At airway branchpoints, the majority of inhaled soluble antigens were captured by CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs rather than DCs.
source: We found that at these regions, the majority of inhaled soluble antigens were captured by CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs rather than DCs.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and flow cytometry data showing differential antigen uptake.

claim: Frequent contacts were observed between CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs and DCs.
source: We observed frequent contacts between CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs and DCs, suggesting the possibility of antigen transfer to DCs.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing physical contacts between these cell types.

claim: CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs are capable of antigen processing and presentation.
source: Yet CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs themselves were capable of antigen processing and presentation, activated T cells in vitro, and interacted with T cells recruited to the airways in an asthma model.
evidence: This is supported by Y-Ae antibody staining data showing antigen presentation.

claim: CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs activated T cells in vitro.
source: Yet CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs themselves were capable of antigen processing and presentation, activated T cells in vitro, and interacted with T cells recruited to the airways in an asthma model.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-culture experiments showing T cell proliferation and cytokine production.

claim: CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs interacted with T cells recruited to the airways in an asthma model.
source: Yet CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs themselves were capable of antigen processing and presentation, activated T cells in vitro, and interacted with T cells recruited to the airways in an asthma model.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data showing sustained interactions between BAMs and T cells.

claim: CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs did not migrate to the draining lymph node and remained lung resident.
source: Unlike DCs, CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs did not migrate to the draining lymph node and remained lung resident.
evidence: This is supported by CCR7 expression data, lymphatic vessel imaging, and lymph node analysis.

claim: CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs located near the bronchial airways are tissue-resident sentinel APCs that are able to drive local allergic inflammation.
source: We therefore propose that CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs located near the bronchial airways are tissue-resident sentinel APCs that are able to drive local allergic inflammation, whereas DCs may be more critical for priming T cell responses in lymph nodes.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing antigen capture, presentation, T cell activation, and lack of migration.

claim: DCs may be more critical for priming T cell responses in lymph nodes.
source: We therefore propose that CX3CR1+ CD11c+ MHC-II+ IMs located near the bronchial airways are tissue-resident sentinel APCs that are able to drive local allergic inflammation, whereas DCs may be more critical for priming T cell responses in lymph nodes.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed migratory behavior of DCs to lymph nodes.

claim: Peribronchial inflammation is a hallmark of asthma that is recapitulated in mouse models of allergic airway disease.
source: Peribronchial inflammation is a hallmark of asthma that is recapitulated in mouse models of allergic airway disease.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about asthma pathology and mouse models.

claim: Foci of leukocytes near the bronchi include numerous eosinophils.
source: Foci of leukocytes can be observed near the bronchi that include numerous eosinophils.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In a classical OVA model of allergic airway disease, foci of leukocytes were not evenly distributed along the airway, but rather were typically located near airway branchpoints and associated with large blood vessels.
source: In our own studies of mouse models of allergic airway disease, such as in a classical model with OVA as an allergen (Daubeuf and Frossard, 2013), we observed in thin cryosections that these foci were not evenly distributed along the airway, but rather were typically located near airway branchpoints and associated with large blood vessels (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Collagen-rich regions near some bifurcating airways contain dense accumulations of collagen surrounding blood vessels.
source: Our imaging revealed regions near some airway branchpoints with dense accumulations of collagen surrounding blood vessels (Figure 1B and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: Collagen-rich regions near some airway branchpoints likely represent bronchovascular bundles which are known to contain bronchi and arteries in a common adventitial sheath.
source: These regions likely represent bronchovascular bundles which are known to contain bronchi and arteries in a common adventitial sheath (Townsley, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed anatomy and a citation to previous literature on lung anatomy.

claim: Bifurcating blood vessels were visible at some collagen-rich sites in which the airways appeared to undergo planar bifurcation.
source: Bifurcating blood vessels, visualized by membrane-bound tdTomato, were also visible at some collagen-rich sites in which the airways appeared to undergo planar bifurcation (Metzger et al., 2008; Figure 1B and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1, and a citation to previous literature on airway branching.

claim: At collagen-rich regions near some bifurcating airways, dense accumulations of myeloid cells were observed in both OVA and house dust mite (HDM) models of allergic airway disease.
source: At the collagen-rich regions near some bifurcating airways, we observed dense accumulations of myeloid cells in both OVA and house dust mite (HDM) models of allergic airway disease (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: In naïve mice, a sparse population of MacGreen+ cells was observed at collagen-rich regions near bifurcating airways.
source: Interestingly, in naïve mice, a sparse population of MacGreen+ cells was also observed at these collagen-rich regions near bifurcating airways (Figure 1E), suggesting that myeloid cells may localize to these areas prior to the formation of foci of leukocytes during inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Myeloid cells may localize to collagen-rich regions near bifurcating airways prior to the formation of foci of leukocytes during inflammation.
source: Interestingly, in naïve mice, a sparse population of MacGreen+ cells was also observed at these collagen-rich regions near bifurcating airways (Figure 1E), suggesting that myeloid cells may localize to these areas prior to the formation of foci of leukocytes during inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of myeloid cells in naïve mice at sites where inflammation occurs.

claim: In naïve mice, clusters of bright CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs and CD11c-YFP+ DCs were observed at some airway bifurcations in collagen-rich regions.
source: In naïve mice, we observed clusters of bright CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs and CD11c-YFP+ DCs at some airway bifurcations in collagen-rich regions (Figure 1F and H, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 1F and H, and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: Scattered bright CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs were observed underneath the entire bronchial airway epithelium.
source: Scattered bright CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs were also observed underneath the entire bronchial airway epithelium (Figure 1F and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 1F and Video 2.

claim: Bright CX3CR1-GFP+ cells were more abundant at the airways than at the alveoli.
source: Bright CX3CR1-GFP+ cells were more abundant at the airways than at the alveoli (Figure 1G)
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cell density shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Bright CD11c-YFP+ DCs were only rarely observed at the alveoli in naïve mice.
source: and bright CD11c-YFP+ DCs were only rarely observed at the alveoli in naïve mice (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cell density shown in Figure 1I.

claim: In the steady-state in the absence of inflammation, both IMs and DCs are located near bronchial airways and may be particularly enriched in collagen-rich regions near bifurcations.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that in the steady-state in the absence of inflammation, both IMs and DCs are located near bronchial airways and may be particularly enriched in collagen-rich regions near bifurcations.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the microscopy data showing the localization of IMs and DCs.

claim: Collagen-rich regions near bifurcations correspond to the sites where eosinophils and other leukocytes accumulate in allergic airway disease.
source: These regions correspond to the sites where eosinophils and other leukocytes accumulate in allergic airway disease, suggesting a potential role for these IMs and/or DCs in the initiation of the local inflammatory response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-localization of IMs/DCs and inflammatory cells.

claim: Numerous bright CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs located near the bronchial airways had taken up fluorescent OVA 1-2 hr after intranasal instillation.
source: Our analysis revealed numerous bright CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs located near the bronchial airways that had taken up fluorescent OVA (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Bright OVA+ CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs had a dendritic morphology, extending long processes under the bronchial airway epithelium.
source: These bright OVA+ CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs had a dendritic morphology, extending long processes under the bronchial airway epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations of cell morphology.

claim: Soluble antigen was taken up at the alveoli, primarily by AMs which had a distinct spherical appearance.
source: As expected, soluble antigen was also taken up at the alveoli, primarily by AMs which had a distinct spherical appearance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs with a dendritic morphology readily captured soluble antigen from the bronchial airway lumen and were distinct from AMs.
source: Thus, CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs with a dendritic morphology readily captured soluble antigen from the bronchial airway lumen and were distinct from AMs.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the microscopy data showing antigen uptake and morphological differences.

claim: CD11c-YFP+ DCs at the airways did not visibly appear to capture OVA by microscopy.
source: In contrast to the CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs near the bronchial airways, the CD11c-YFP+ DCs at these sites did not visibly appear to capture OVA by microscopy (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: OVA was preferentially captured by bright CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs rather than bright CD11c-YFP+ DCs.
source: Our imaging of dual reporter mice confirmed that OVA was preferentially captured by bright CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs rather than bright CD11c-YFP+ DCs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CD11c-YFP+ DCs captured much smaller amounts of OVA than CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs.
source: Quantification of OVA uptake indicated that CD11c-YFP+ DCs captured much smaller amounts of OVA than CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of fluorescence intensity shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Bright CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs preferentially took up fluorescently labelled extracts from HDM.
source: We also observed preferential uptake of fluorescently labelled extracts from HDM, a relevant aeroallergen, by bright CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Bright CX3CR1-GFP+ and bright CD11c-YFP+ cells were largely non-overlapping populations.
source: Our imaging also confirmed that bright CX3CR1-GFP+ and bright CD11c-YFP+ cells were largely non-overlapping populations (Figure 2D and F).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and F.

claim: Some of the bright CX3CR1-GFP+ cells did have dim expression of CD11c-YFP, and vice versa.
source: When we increased the image contrast, we observed that some of the bright CX3CR1-GFP+ cells did have dim expression of CD11c-YFP, and vice versa, as expected from previous studies (Jung et al., 2000; Sen et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and citations to previous literature.

claim: Rare cells were observed that were bright for both the CX3CR1-GFP and CD11c-YFP reporters.
source: Occasionally, we also observed rare cells that were bright for both the CX3CR1-GFP and CD11c-YFP reporters, yet the majority of cells in the naïve state appeared to be bright for only one of these reporters suggesting they were distinct cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The majority of cells in the naïve state appeared to be bright for only one of the CX3CR1-GFP or CD11c-YFP reporters suggesting they were distinct cell types.
source: Occasionally, we also observed rare cells that were bright for both the CX3CR1-GFP and CD11c-YFP reporters, yet the majority of cells in the naïve state appeared to be bright for only one of these reporters suggesting they were distinct cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the microscopy data showing largely non-overlapping expression of the two reporters.

claim: CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs had a dendritic morphology.
source: Indeed, CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs had a dendritic morphology as we had noted above, whereas CD11c-YFP+ DCs were rounder and did not appear to extend long processes.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations of cell morphology.

claim: CD11c-YFP+ DCs were rounder and did not appear to extend long processes.
source: Indeed, CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs had a dendritic morphology as we had noted above, whereas CD11c-YFP+ DCs were rounder and did not appear to extend long processes.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations of cell morphology.

claim: CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs had lower sphericity values compared to CD11c-YFP+ DCs.
source: CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs had lower sphericity values (Figure 2G) and increased mean lengths of their longest axes (Figure 2H) compared to CD11c-YFP+ DCs.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cell shape shown in Figure 2G.

claim: CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs had increased mean lengths of their longest axes compared to CD11c-YFP+ DCs.
source: CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs had lower sphericity values (Figure 2G) and increased mean lengths of their longest axes (Figure 2H) compared to CD11c-YFP+ DCs.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cell shape shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The disparity in morphology and antigen uptake capacity suggests that CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs and CD11c-YFP+ DCs are two distinct cell populations present in airway-adjacent areas in the steady state.
source: The disparity in morphology and antigen uptake capacity suggests that CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs and CD11c-YFP+ DCs are two distinct cell populations present in airway-adjacent areas in the steady state, and that CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs are the primary antigen capturing cell type at the airways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in morphology and antigen uptake.

claim: CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs are the primary antigen capturing cell type at the airways.
source: The disparity in morphology and antigen uptake capacity suggests that CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs and CD11c-YFP+ DCs are two distinct cell populations present in airway-adjacent areas in the steady state, and that CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs are the primary antigen capturing cell type at the airways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed superior antigen uptake by IMs compared to DCs.

claim: The average intensity of fluorescent OVA was over three-fold brighter in CX3CR1-GFPbright IMs compared with CD11c-YFPbright DCs by flow cytometry.
source: This analysis confirmed that the average intensity of fluorescent OVA was over three-fold brighter in CX3CR1-GFPbright IMs compared with CD11c-YFPbright DCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: When gated specifically on OVAbright MHC-II+ cells by flow cytometry, the majority of cells were CX3CR1-GFPbright but not CD11c-YFPbright.
source: Indeed, when we gated specifically on OVAbright MHC-II+ cells by flow cytometry, the majority of cells were CX3CR1-GFPbright but not CD11c-YFPbright (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: DCs take up low amounts of soluble antigen from the bronchial airway lumen.
source: Therefore, our results show that DCs also take up soluble antigen from the bronchial airway lumen, but that the majority of antigen is taken up by a distinct population of CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing some OVA uptake by DCs, though less than BAMs.

claim: The majority of antigen is taken up by a distinct population of CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs.
source: Therefore, our results show that DCs also take up soluble antigen from the bronchial airway lumen, but that the majority of antigen is taken up by a distinct population of CX3CR1-GFP+ IMs.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and flow cytometry data showing superior antigen uptake by IMs.

claim: The CX3CR1-GFPbright OVAbright cells were predominantly MHC-IIhi and CD11cmid.
source: After administering fluorescent OVA intranasally and then isolating and enzymatically digesting the lungs, our flow cytometric analysis showed that the CX3CR1-GFPbright OVAbright cells were predominantly MHC-IIhi and CD11cmid (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The presence of CX3CR1-GFPbright OVAbright cells in naïve mice and high MHC-II expression suggested they were not derived from inflammatory monocytes.
source: The presence of these cells in naïve mice and high MHC-II expression suggested they were not derived from inflammatory monocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of these cells in naïve mice and their high MHC-II expression.

claim: The CX3CR1-GFPbright OVAbright cells predominantly expressed the macrophage markers CD64 and MerTK.
source: The CX3CR1-GFPbright OVAbright cells also predominantly expressed the macrophage markers CD64 and MerTK, and had relatively low to undetectable staining for the cDC marker CD24 (Figure 3A and B), consistent with surface markers previously established for IMs (Gautier et al., 2012; Guilliams et al., 2013; Schlitzer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and B, and citations to previous literature on IM markers.

claim: The CX3CR1-GFPbright OVAbright cells had relatively low to undetectable staining for the cDC marker CD24.
source: The CX3CR1-GFPbright OVAbright cells also predominantly expressed the macrophage markers CD64 and MerTK, and had relatively low to undetectable staining for the cDC marker CD24 (Figure 3A and B), consistent with surface markers previously established for IMs (Gautier et al., 2012; Guilliams et al., 2013; Schlitzer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and B, and citations to previous literature on IM markers.

claim: The majority of the CD11c-YFPbright cells were MHC-II+, CD11cmid-hi and CD24hi but did not express CD64 and MerTK, thus representing cDCs.
source: Conversely, the majority of the CD11c-YFPbright cells were MHC-II+, CD11cmid-hi and CD24hi but did not express CD64 and MerTK, thus representing cDCs (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: CD64+ OVAbright cells were largely CD11c-YFP– but did express surface CD11c by antibody staining.
source: Notably, CD64+ OVAbright cells were largely CD11c-YFP– but did express surface CD11c by antibody staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), albeit with reduced abundance compared to cDCs, indicating the expression of the CD11c-YFP transgene is more restricted to DCs than the CD11c protein, consistent with a prior study (Rodero et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The expression of the CD11c-YFP transgene is more restricted to DCs than the CD11c protein.
source: Notably, CD64+ OVAbright cells were largely CD11c-YFP– but did express surface CD11c by antibody staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), albeit with reduced abundance compared to cDCs, indicating the expression of the CD11c-YFP transgene is more restricted to DCs than the CD11c protein, consistent with a prior study (Rodero et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the flow cytometry data and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Monocytes and the CX3CR1-GFP+ subset of cDC2s all had lower CX3CR1-GFP expression than the MHC-II+ CD64+ MerTK+ cells.
source: We found that monocytes, which resolve into two subsets based on CX3CR1-GFP expression (Geissmann et al., 2003), and the CX3CR1-GFP+ subset of cDC2s, all had lower CX3CR1-GFP expression than the MHC-II+ CD64+ MerTK+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), consistent with our imaging data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The CX3CR1-GFPbright cells observed near the bronchial airway epithelium by microscopy were represented by the CX3CR1-GFPbright CD64+ MHC-II+ IMs identified by flow cytometry.
source: To indeed verify that the CX3CR1-GFPbright cells we had observed near the bronchial airway epithelium by microscopy were represented by the CX3CR1-GFPbright CD64+ MHC-II+ IMs identified by flow cytometry, we stained precision-cut thick lung slices from CX3CR1-GFP or CD11c-YFP mice with antibodies against CD64 and MHC-II.
evidence: This is supported by antibody staining and microscopy data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The CX3CR1-GFPbright cells located near the bronchial airways were CD64+.
source: By two-photon microscopy, we confirmed that the CX3CR1-GFPbright cells located near the bronchial airways were CD64+ (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The CD11c-YFPbright cells were CD64-negative.
source: In contrast, the CD11c-YFPbright cells were CD64-negative (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Most of the CX3CR1-GFPbright cells located near the airways were MHC-II+.
source: Most of the CX3CR1-GFPbright cells located near the airways were MHC-II+ (Figure 3C solid arrowheads and Figure 3D), although occasional MHC-IIlo/— cells were also visualized (Figure 3C, open arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Occasional MHC-IIlo/— CX3CR1-GFPbright cells were visualized near the airways.
source: Most of the CX3CR1-GFPbright cells located near the airways were MHC-II+ (Figure 3C solid arrowheads and Figure 3D), although occasional MHC-IIlo/— cells were also visualized (Figure 3C, open arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The majority of the CX3CR1-GFPbright cells localized near the bronchial airway epithelium that capture soluble inhaled antigens are CD11c+ CD64+ MHC-II+ IMs.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that the majority of the CX3CR1-GFPbright cells localized near the bronchial airway epithelium that capture soluble inhaled antigens are CD11c+ CD64+ MHC-II+ IMs.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the flow cytometry and microscopy data.

claim: This subset of IMs is referred to as Bronchus-Associated Macrophages (BAMs) based on their spatial localization near the bronchial airways.
source: Based on their spatial localization near the bronchial airways, we propose that this subset of IMs be referred to as Bronchus-Associated Macrophages (BAMs).
evidence: This is a nomenclature proposal based on the observed anatomical localization.

claim: CD64+ MHC-II+ BAMs had high surface expression of CD11b and were uniformly MerTK+.
source: CD64+ MHC-II+ BAMs had high surface expression of CD11b and were uniformly MerTK+, but had only minimal expression of a Zbtb46-GFP reporter that was nearly 10-fold lower than CD24+ DCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C), further confirming these cells are not DCs despite sharing similar markers to cDC2s.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: CD64+ MHC-II+ BAMs had only minimal expression of a Zbtb46-GFP reporter that was nearly 10-fold lower than CD24+ DCs.
source: CD64+ MHC-II+ BAMs had high surface expression of CD11b and were uniformly MerTK+, but had only minimal expression of a Zbtb46-GFP reporter that was nearly 10-fold lower than CD24+ DCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C), further confirming these cells are not DCs despite sharing similar markers to cDC2s.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: BAMs are not DCs despite sharing similar markers to cDC2s.
source: CD64+ MHC-II+ BAMs had high surface expression of CD11b and were uniformly MerTK+, but had only minimal expression of a Zbtb46-GFP reporter that was nearly 10-fold lower than CD24+ DCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C), further confirming these cells are not DCs despite sharing similar markers to cDC2s.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low Zbtb46-GFP expression in BAMs compared to DCs.

claim: CD64+ MHC-II+ BAMs had low CD169 expression that partially overlapped with background staining.
source: Whereas AMs had high surface expression of CD169 and Siglec-F as expected, we found that CD64+ MHC-II+ BAMs had low CD169 expression that partially overlapped with background staining, and did not express Siglec-F (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and F), further supporting that these are two distinct macrophage populations.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: CD64+ MHC-II+ BAMs did not express Siglec-F.
source: Whereas AMs had high surface expression of CD169 and Siglec-F as expected, we found that CD64+ MHC-II+ BAMs had low CD169 expression that partially overlapped with background staining, and did not express Siglec-F (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and F), further supporting that these are two distinct macrophage populations.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: BAMs and AMs are two distinct macrophage populations.
source: Whereas AMs had high surface expression of CD169 and Siglec-F as expected, we found that CD64+ MHC-II+ BAMs had low CD169 expression that partially overlapped with background staining, and did not express Siglec-F (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and F), further supporting that these are two distinct macrophage populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression of CD169 and Siglec-F.

claim: One major cluster of IMs was detected by scRNAseq, marked by the highest density of expression of Cx3cr1.
source: One major cluster of IMs was detected, marked by the highest density of expression of Cx3cr1, consistent with our imaging analysis (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The IM cluster had high expression of Mafb.
source: The IM cluster also had high expression of Mafb (Figure 4B), which is thought to largely be restricted to cells of the macrophage lineage (Wu et al., 2016), with the exception of AMs (Gautier et al., 2012; Gibbings et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4B and citations to previous literature.

claim: Mafb is thought to largely be restricted to cells of the macrophage lineage, with the exception of AMs.
source: The IM cluster also had high expression of Mafb (Figure 4B), which is thought to largely be restricted to cells of the macrophage lineage (Wu et al., 2016), with the exception of AMs (Gautier et al., 2012; Gibbings et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on Mafb expression.

claim: BAMs make up the majority of the population of IMs.
source: Within the major IM cluster two distinct populations were visible. BAMs make up the majority of the population of IMs, which expressed comparable amounts of H2-Ab1 (MHC-II) to the DC subsets, consistent with our flow cytometric analysis, as well as Itgax (CD11c), Mmp12 and Ccr2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data showing the relative abundance of BAMs within the IM cluster.

claim: BAMs expressed comparable amounts of H2-Ab1 (MHC-II) to the DC subsets.
source: Within the major IM cluster two distinct populations were visible. BAMs make up the majority of the population of IMs, which expressed comparable amounts of H2-Ab1 (MHC-II) to the DC subsets, consistent with our flow cytometric analysis, as well as Itgax (CD11c), Mmp12 and Ccr2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A minor population of IMs was visible with high expression of Lyve1 and Folr2, with weaker expression of H2-Ab1 and Itgax.
source: A minor population of IMs was visible with high expression of Lyve1 and Folr2, with weaker expression of H2-Ab1 and Itgax (Figure 4B), consistent with previous reports (Chakarov et al., 2019; Schyns et al., 2019; Ural et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4B and citations to previous literature.

claim: Mrc1 (CD206) was widely expressed among IMs, with the highest expression on the Lyve1+ population.
source: Mrc1 (CD206) was widely expressed among IMs, with the highest expression on the Lyve1+ population (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Siglec1 (CD169) was only detected in a small fraction of cells in the IM cluster.
source: Siglec1 (CD169) was only detected in a small fraction of cells in the IM cluster (Figure 4B), suggesting reads were near the threshold for detection, consistent with our CD169 staining by flow cytometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Several clusters of DCs were identified by a high density of expression of Flt3 and Zbtb46.
source: Several clusters of DCs were identified by a high density of expression of Flt3 and Zbtb46 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DC clusters showed differential expression of Mgl2, Cd207, and Ccr7, suggesting they represented cDC2s, cDC1s, and migratory DCs, respectively.
source: These clusters showed differential expression of Mgl2, Cd207, and Ccr7, suggesting they represented cDC2s, cDC1s, and migratory DCs, respectively (Izumi et al., 2021; Sichien et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4C and citations to previous literature on DC markers.

claim: Genes most highly expressed in IMs compared to AMs and DCs included genes encoding chemokines (Cxcl13, Ccl7, and Ccl2), complement pathway components (C1q genes and C3ar1), Apoe, and Mmp12.
source: Several genes were identified that were most highly expressed in IMs compared to AMs and DCs: these included genes encoding chemokines (Cxcl13, Ccl7, and Ccl2), complement pathway components (C1q genes and C3ar1), Apoe, and Mmp12 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: BAMs, AMs, and DCs are functionally distinct subsets of cells based on transcriptional profile analysis.
source: This transcriptional profile analysis demonstrates that despite similarities in their surface marker profiles, BAMs, AMs, and DCs are functionally distinct subsets of cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the scRNAseq data showing distinct gene expression patterns.

claim: BAMs had intermediate CD206 surface expression in a Gaussian distribution by flow cytometry.
source: Our flow cytometric analysis of CD64+ MHC-II+ cells showed that BAMs had intermediate CD206 surface expression in a Gaussian distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The CX3CR1-GFPbright BAMs that predominantly captured antigen (OVA) near the airways were CD206+.
source: By two-photon microscopy of precision-cut thick lung slices, we observed that the CX3CR1-GFPbright BAMs that predominantly captured antigen (OVA) near the airways were CD206+ (Figure 5A), although the expression of CD206 was variable.
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CX3CR1-GFPbright MHC-IIhi cells near the airways expressed variable intermediate amounts of CD206.
source: By co-staining with MHC-II, we observed that CX3CR1-GFPbright MHC-IIhi cells near the airways (Figure 5B, solid arrowheads) expressed variable intermediate amounts of CD206, whereas the highest CD206 expression was observed on some CX3CR1-GFP+MHC-IIlo cells that were also located near the airways (Figure 5B, open arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The highest CD206 expression was observed on some CX3CR1-GFP+MHC-IIlo cells that were also located near the airways.
source: By co-staining with MHC-II, we observed that CX3CR1-GFPbright MHC-IIhi cells near the airways (Figure 5B, solid arrowheads) expressed variable intermediate amounts of CD206, whereas the highest CD206 expression was observed on some CX3CR1-GFP+MHC-IIlo cells that were also located near the airways (Figure 5B, open arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: BAMs, which capture antigen near the airways and are MHC-II+, express variable amounts of CD206.
source: Taken together, these data establish that BAMs, which capture antigen near the airways and are MHC-II+, express variable amounts of CD206.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the flow cytometry and microscopy data.

claim: Nerves were readily visualized near the bronchial airways and at airway branchpoints where BAMs were abundant.
source: By two-photon microscopy of precision-cut thick lung slices stained with an antibody to L1CAM, a neuronal cell adhesion molecule (Rathjen and Schachner, 1984; Tacke et al., 1987), we readily visualized nerves near the bronchial airways and at airway branchpoints where BAMs were abundant (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D, and citations to previous literature on L1CAM.

claim: A subset of BAMs were directly in contact with nerves, while other BAMs were not in contact with nerves.
source: A subset of BAMs were directly in contact with nerves, while other BAMs were not in contact with nerves (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Punctate CD169 staining on BAMs was only detectable above background in a subset of cells.
source: In two-photon microscopy of precision-cut thick lung slices, we observed punctate CD169 staining on BAMs that was only detectable above background in a subset of cells (Figure 5D, solid arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cells with bright uniform CD169 staining in contact with nerves were not CX3CR1-GFPbright and thus were distinct from BAMs.
source: In contrast, we occasionally observed cells with bright uniform CD169 staining in contact with nerves; however, these cells were not CX3CR1-GFPbright and thus were distinct from BAMs (Figure 5D, open arrowhead).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The punctate CD169 staining on BAMs was polarized toward one side of the cell, and this often seemed to be at the interface with a CD11c-YFP+ DC.
source: Interestingly, the punctate CD169 staining on BAMs was polarized toward one side of the cell, and this often seemed to be at the interface with a CD11c-YFP+ DC (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CD169 plays an important role in cell-cell contacts between macrophages and DCs in the spleen and lymph nodes, which enhanced antigen transfer and cross-presentation.
source: A previous study demonstrated an important role for CD169 in cell-cell contacts between macrophages and DCs in the spleen and lymph nodes, which enhanced antigen transfer and cross-presentation (van Dinther et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature on CD169 function.

claim: BAMs and DCs were frequently in contact in static imaging.
source: In our static imaging data above, we noted that BAMs and DCs were frequently in contact (see Figure 2D and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Extensive, dynamic interactions were observed between BAMs and DCs in time-lapse imaging of precision-cut lung slices by two-photon microscopy.
source: We observed extensive, dynamic interactions between BAMs and DCs in time-lapse imaging of precision-cut lung slices by two-photon microscopy (Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Video 4.

claim: BAMs may transfer antigen, or peptide-MHC II complexes, to DCs.
source: This suggests the possibility that BAMs may transfer antigen, or peptide-MHC II complexes, to DCs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed interactions between BAMs and DCs and CD169 localization.

claim: BAMs may interact with nerves.
source: Taken together, in addition to their role in antigen capture from the airways, BAMs may interact with nerves and/or communicate with DCs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed proximity of some BAMs to nerves.

claim: A large majority (~80%) of BAMs had taken up OVA 2 hr after intranasal administration.
source: Indeed, a large majority (~80%) of BAMs gated by these markers had taken up OVA, whereas a smaller proportion (~50%) of cDC2s and less than 5% of monocytes were OVA+ (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A smaller proportion (~50%) of cDC2s had taken up OVA 2 hr after intranasal administration.
source: Indeed, a large majority (~80%) of BAMs gated by these markers had taken up OVA, whereas a smaller proportion (~50%) of cDC2s and less than 5% of monocytes were OVA+ (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Less than 5% of monocytes were OVA+ 2 hr after intranasal administration.
source: Indeed, a large majority (~80%) of BAMs gated by these markers had taken up OVA, whereas a smaller proportion (~50%) of cDC2s and less than 5% of monocytes were OVA+ (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CX3CR1-GFP+ BAMs took up soluble fluorescent molecules of a range of sizes, such as TRITC-dextran molecules that were 10 kDa or 155 kDa, as well as phycoerythrin (PE), a 240 kDa molecule.
source: By microscopy, we observed that in addition to soluble OVA and HDM extract, CX3CR1-GFP+ BAMs took up other soluble fluorescent molecules of a range of sizes, such as TRITC-dextran molecules that were 10 kDa or 155 kDa, as well as phycoerythrin (PE), a 240 kDa molecule (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: A greater proportion of BAMs were FITC-DX+ when smaller molecules were instilled compared to larger molecules.
source: We found that a greater proportion of BAMs were FITC-DX+ when smaller molecules were instilled compared to larger molecules (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The magnitude of antigen uptake by BAMs is inversely related to the antigen size.
source: Therefore, the magnitude of antigen uptake by BAMs is inversely related to the antigen size.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the flow cytometry data showing size-dependent uptake.

claim: Bead capture by CX3CR1-GFP+ BAMs or CD11c-YFP+ DCs near the airways was rarely observed.
source: However, we rarely observed bead capture by CX3CR1-GFP+ BAMs or CD11c-YFP+ DCs near the airways (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In the alveolar space, beads were taken up primarily by highly spherical cells that were dimly CD11c-YFP+.
source: In contrast, in the alveolar space, beads were taken up primarily by highly spherical cells that were dimly CD11c-YFP+ (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The highly spherical cells that were dimly CD11c-YFP+ and took up beads in the alveolar space were AMs, not DCs.
source: By location and morphology, we concluded that these cells were AMs, not DCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location, morphology, and CD11c-YFP expression of the cells.

claim: BAMs preferentially captured soluble antigens.
source: In summary, BAMs preferentially captured soluble antigens, whereas both BAMs and DCs residing at the airway interstitium showed minimal capture of beads.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the microscopy data showing differential uptake of soluble antigens versus beads.

claim: Both BAMs and DCs residing at the airway interstitium showed minimal capture of beads.
source: In summary, BAMs preferentially captured soluble antigens, whereas both BAMs and DCs residing at the airway interstitium showed minimal capture of beads.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the microscopy data showing minimal bead uptake.

claim: Both BAMs and cDC2s stained with the Y-Ae antibody, demonstrating that BAMs processed and presented antigen.
source: Both BAMs and cDC2s stained with the Y-Ae antibody by flow cytometry (Figure 7A), demonstrating that BAMs processed and presented antigen, like DCs, rather than simply degrading it.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: BAMs processed and presented antigen, like DCs, rather than simply degrading it.
source: Both BAMs and cDC2s stained with the Y-Ae antibody by flow cytometry (Figure 7A), demonstrating that BAMs processed and presented antigen, like DCs, rather than simply degrading it.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Y-Ae antibody staining data.

claim: Brighter Y-Ae staining was observed on BAMs compared with cDC2s.
source: Brighter Y-Ae staining was observed on BAMs compared with cDC2s (Figure 7A), consistent with the superior soluble antigen uptake we had observed (Figures 2 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: AMs showed negligible Y-Ae staining.
source: AMs, with low MHC-II expression and a high degradative capacity, showed negligible Y-Ae staining (Figure 7A), confirming these are not the relevant APCs for CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: AMs are not the relevant APCs for CD4 T cells.
source: AMs, with low MHC-II expression and a high degradative capacity, showed negligible Y-Ae staining (Figure 7A), confirming these are not the relevant APCs for CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the negligible Y-Ae staining on AMs.

claim: BAMs had higher surface expression of the co-stimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 compared to cDC2s.
source: We also tested whether BAMs could provide the necessary co-stimulatory signals for T cell activation and found that BAMs had higher surface expression of the co-stimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 compared to cDC2s (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: BAMs induced the robust proliferation of naïve OT-II T cells when cultured in the presence of OVA peptide.
source: When cultured in the presence of OVA peptide, BAMs induced the robust proliferation of naïve OT-II T cells, albeit somewhat less efficiently than cDC2s, as expected, given the high efficiency of naïve T cell activation by DCs (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-culture data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: BAMs induced naïve OT-II T cell proliferation somewhat less efficiently than cDC2s.
source: When cultured in the presence of OVA peptide, BAMs induced the robust proliferation of naïve OT-II T cells, albeit somewhat less efficiently than cDC2s, as expected, given the high efficiency of naïve T cell activation by DCs (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-culture data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: BAMs and cDC2s equivalently induced IL-13 production when co-cultured with Th2 polarized, effector OT-II cells and OVA peptide.
source: Interestingly, BAMs and cDC2s equivalently induced IL-13 production when co-cultured with Th2 polarized, effector OT-II cells and OVA peptide (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-culture data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: BAMs possess the necessary machinery for antigen presentation and activation of T cells.
source: These findings indicate that BAMs possess the necessary machinery for antigen presentation and activation of T cells, and further suggest that BAMs may equivalently activate effector T cells compared with DCs.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the Y-Ae staining, co-stimulatory molecule expression, and T cell activation data.

claim: BAMs may equivalently activate effector T cells compared with DCs.
source: These findings indicate that BAMs possess the necessary machinery for antigen presentation and activation of T cells, and further suggest that BAMs may equivalently activate effector T cells compared with DCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the equivalent IL-13 production induced by BAMs and cDC2s in co-culture with effector T cells.

claim: Sustained interactions were observed between OT-II T cells and CX3CR1-GFP+ BAMs in the lung after allergen challenge.
source: After allergen challenge, we observed sustained interactions between OT-II T cells and CX3CR1-GFP+ BAMs in the lung (Figure 7E–G, Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 7E-G and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: Interactions between BAMs and OT-II T cells were comparable to the interactions reported during antigen-specific T cell activation by DCs in the lymph nodes.
source: These interactions between BAMs and OT-II T cells were comparable to the interactions reported during antigen-specific T cell activation by DCs in the lymph nodes (Mempel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature on T cell-DC interactions, supported by a citation.

claim: Some OT-II T cells engaged in sustained interactions with CD11c-YFP+ DCs near the airways.
source: Some OT-II T cells were also observed to engage in sustained interactions with CD11c-YFP+ DCs near the airways (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations mentioned in the text.

claim: Both BAMs and DCs can serve as APCs for the local activation of effector T cells in lung peribronchial regions.
source: These observations suggest that both BAMs and DCs can serve as APCs for the local activation of effector T cells in lung peribronchial regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed interactions between T cells and both BAMs and DCs.

claim: BAMs had dendrites that were continuously extended and probing, but their cell bodies showed very minimal displacement over time.
source: BAMs had dendrites that were continuously extended and probing, but their cell bodies showed very minimal displacement over time.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy observations of BAM dynamics.

claim: DCs were surveying their surroundings by moving their entire cell bodies and traversed greater distances than BAMs.
source: In contrast, DCs were surveying their surroundings by moving their entire cell bodies and traversed greater distances than BAMs (Figure 8A–D and Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 8A-D and Video 7.

claim: DCs were highly migratory whereas BAMs were probing by extending dendrites with little net movement.
source: Therefore, DCs were highly migratory whereas BAMs were probing by extending dendrites with little net movement.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the time-lapse microscopy data showing differential motility.

claim: After 4 hr of LPS exposure, CCR7 was upregulated on a significant proportion of DCs in a dose-dependent manner, but not on BAMs.
source: After 4 hr, we found that CCR7 was upregulated on a significant proportion of DCs in a dose-dependent manner, but not on BAMs (Figure 8E–F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8E-F.

claim: After OVA challenge, DCs upregulated CCR7 expression in previously sensitized mice but not in naïve mice exposed to OVA for the first time.
source: Indeed, after OVA challenge, DCs upregulated CCR7 expression in previously sensitized mice but not in naïve mice exposed to OVA for the first time (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: BAMs did not upregulate CCR7 in either sensitized or naïve mice after OVA challenge.
source: Conversely, BAMs did not upregulate CCR7 in either sensitized or naïve mice (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The expression of CCR7 only on the DCs, but not BAMs, would likely allow DCs to selectively migrate to the lymph node.
source: As such, the expression of CCR7 only on the DCs, but not BAMs, would likely allow DCs to selectively migrate to the lymph node.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of CCR7 in lymph node migration and the differential CCR7 expression.

claim: After intranasal instillation of HDM or LPS, CD11c-YFP+ cells, but not CX3CR1-GFP+ cells, were frequently observed migrating within lung lymphatics.
source: After intranasal instillation of HDM or LPS, we frequently observed CD11c-YFP+ cells, but not CX3CR1-GFP+ cells, migrating within lung lymphatics (Figure 8H, Videos 8 and 9).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 8H and Videos 8 and 9.

claim: A population of CD64+ MHC-II+ cells that were Ly6C+ were recruited to the draining mediastinal lymph node 1 d after HDM and PE administration.
